title: WLPA: A Network Management Framework for Allocating Scarce Quantum-Safe Link Postures under Weakest-Link Exposure
abstract: Network operators migrating distributed systems to post-quantum and quantum-safe cryptography face a resource-management problem: quantum key distribution (QKD) gives the strongest guarantee available but is hardware-scarce and costly, so only a fraction of a deployment's links can receive it. Default practice -- ranking links by traffic or centrality and upgrading the top scorers -- optimizes each link in isolation, while a distributed job's real security is set by whichever active link ends up weakest. We present WLPA (Weakest-Link Posture Assignment), an implementation-ready decision framework and algorithm for allocating scarce quantum-safe postures under hardware, latency, and compliance constraints. WLPA computes the optimal weakest-link posture in closed form and returns an assignment in O(|E| log |E|) time -- 125 ms for a 20,000-link network on a laptop -- with a breach-aware refinement matching an exact integer program under common conditions. Our central contribution is a dichotomy telling operators exactly when existing per-link heuristics already match this optimum and when they systematically fail: under constant upgrade cost and uniform traffic-driven risk the two coincide exactly; once costs vary or an adversary concentrates on weak targets, heuristics leave the weakest link unprotected, unboundedly. We validate WLPA across 19 experiments: four microservice topologies, a real enterprise network (SNAP email-Eu-core), a post-quantum latency benchmark, a Qiskit BB84 simulation and a real-hardware BB84 run on IBM's ibm_marrakesh processor, checks against real production traffic traces, a CVE-calibrated correlated-compromise study, Bayesian uncertainty quantification, and seven baseline methods. A concrete-security reduction grounds the framework as theoretical foundation, not primary contribution.
summary: This paper introduces WLPA, a novel, efficient framework for optimally allocating scarce quantum-safe resources like QKD across large networks. It moves beyond simple per-link security assessments by recognizing that system security is limited by the weakest link. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, implementable solution that outperforms standard industry heuristics, especially under sophisticated, targeted attack models.
main_problem: Network operators must allocate scarce, high-security quantum-safe link postures (like QKD) across a distributed system, where overall security is dictated by the single weakest link.
main_result: The authors present WLPA, an algorithm that computes the optimal weakest-link posture assignment in polynomial time, providing a rigorous framework superior to simple per-link heuristics when costs or attack models vary.
method: The core method is developing a closed-form, optimal decision framework (WLPA) that solves a constrained resource allocation problem, validated against integer programming models and various network topologies.
model_or_system: The system is a distributed network modeled as a graph where links ($e \in ED$) require upgrading to specific quantum-safe postures (Level 1, 2, or 3) constrained by a total QKD budget ($B$) and latency limits ($L$).
key_observables: System security (minimum link posture), Breach Probability $B(Q)$, and the optimal achievable security level $S^\star(B, L)$.
important_parameters: QKD Budget ($B$), Latency Budget ($L$), Link Compliance Cap ($c_e$), and the three discrete Link Posture Levels.
main_assumptions: The security derivation relies on a standard hybrid-argument bound, and the framework assumes a specific model for exploit probability schedules ($p(\ell)$) which are model-calibrated.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of job breach probability between WLPA and heuristic methods under varying QKD budgets, and show the near-linear runtime scaling of the WLPA algorithm.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the weakest-link security principle, introduces WLPA as the optimal allocation algorithm, proves its correctness and complexity, presents a dichotomy showing when heuristics fail, and validates the framework across 19 diverse experimental scenarios.
why_interesting: While focused on network engineering, the underlying mathematical structure—optimizing a global minimum subject to local resource constraints—is analogous to finding the weakest point in a quantum computation or communication chain, making the resource allocation theory relevant to quantum network security.

figures.caption: Figure 1: WLPA’s operational loop: identify active links and volumes, assign compliance caps, run the closed-form allocator, deploy starting from the binding link, and re-run on topology or budget change. The allocation step is implemented and validated (Sections 4–5.7); the deploy/enforce step is architected but not built or measured on a live system (Section 6.2)

Figure 1 summarizes the framework: topology and compliance caps feed a closed-form ceiling computation, which sets the system-wide target posture; a floor-raising pass brings every active link to that target; and a breach-aware refinement spends any remaining QKD budget where it reduces breach probability most. This computational pipeline — the part inside the dashed box in Figure 1 — is what we implement and validate throughout this paper (Sections 4–5.7): it runs in O(|E| log |E|) and is fast enough to re-run whenever topology, budget, or compliance requirements change.
